questions.question: Explain why poorer countries often have higher birth rates and death rates than wealthier countries.
questions.expected_answer: Death rates: poverty means malnutrition, unsafe water and poor sanitation, crowded housing and distant, under-resourced clinics, so more people (especially babies and children) die. Birth rates: high child mortality leads parents to have more children; children help with farm and household work and support parents in old age (no pensions); girls may leave school and marry early; family planning is harder to access. In wealthier countries children are expensive, more women study and work, people marry later and contraception is available.

questions.question: Describe the direct and indirect effects of war on population.
questions.expected_answer: Direct: deaths of soldiers and civilians in fighting, bombing and genocide (e.g. Second World War about 70-85 million; Rwanda 1994 about 800 000). Indirect: destruction of farms, roads, water supplies and clinics leads to famine and disease (e.g. most deaths in the DRC war); lower birth rates during war and a baby boom afterwards; imbalance of men and women; mass displacement of refugees and internally displaced people.

questions.question: Define refugee and internally displaced person, and explain how refugee movements affect populations.
questions.expected_answer: Refugee: someone who has fled across an international border because of war, violence or persecution and cannot safely return. Internally displaced person: someone who has fled but stays in their own country. The country of origin loses population, often young adults and skilled workers; host areas (usually neighbouring countries) grow suddenly and must provide shelter, water, food, schooling and health care, which can strain resources, though refugees also bring skills and contribute.
